summary: Scope the one-budget-for-a-prompt design in rota, six questions, each verified adversarially

report.question: List every cap, limit, trim, truncation, eviction and hold from a wake to a model prompt and from a model reply back into the records, with name, constant, file, line, unit, cause and what the seat sees; then say which can fire on the same turn and in what order.
report.summary: I found 31 separate caps on the two paths, and they count five different units. Only one of them, the per-turn total added by frame 43, was derived from the window; every other one is a hand-set number with a night in its comment. The prompt path runs in four stages: each pushed read applies its own private budget, `push_working_set` reshapes some pushes by wake kind, `PUSH_CHARS` caps each pushed key, then `_fit` spends one derived budget in a fixed order of wake cut, middle eviction and exchange cut. The reply path runs the server output cap, the stream stops, the reply cut, the identical-turn stop, then the per-turn result room and the per-result caps in call order, then the withholding, the repeat line and the refusal counter. On one ordinary turn up to fourteen of these can fire, and their order is fixed by the code, not by a design. Three prompt-path constants are now stale against the 16,384 window that every shipped profile pins. The first source read of a turn is an explicit exception to the per-turn total, so the one number a test asserts today already has a hole in it. Record writes also truncate silently at 160, 200, 300 and 460 characters, with no notice to the seat at all.

open_questions: Is the 3.97 characters-to-the-token ratio in _fit_budget (rota/core/runner.py:566) still the measured ratio at a 16,384 window? The docstring says it was measured for these models, but the surrounding arithmetic is written against 12,288.

Does the per-role [context] override still do anything? rota/llm/profiles/local-gemma-critic.toml:37 sets developer = 16384 while the same file's [pins] now sets num_ctx = 16384, so the override may now be a no-op. I did not read profile.py's precedence to confirm.

Is code.area's 10,000 (rota/roles/api.py:6024) deliberately below the 14,000 the PUSH_CHARS comment claims for it, or did one of the two move without the other? The comments disagree and I found no record that settles it.

Does the LiteLLM backend send any window at all? An archived scope note in plans/archive/context-caps-scope-2026-09-18.json says LiteLLMBackend never emits num_ctx, which would make the whole prompt budget provenance-only on those profiles. I did not open LiteLLMBackend to check it today.

Is result_room ever recomputed when _fit evicts between turns? It is computed from transcript[0] after _fit has run, but the wake block it measures may already be a cut one, so the same wake can be charged at two different sizes on two turns.
Are the record-write truncations (160, 200, 300, 460) ever observable? No caller returns the truncated length to the seat, so a verdict whose reason was cut reads as complete in the result.
surprises: The per-turn total's own comment reasons entirely against a 12,288 window: it cites _fit_budget(12288, 4000) = 20,391 and says two capped source reads exceed the budget on 1,367 of 1,367 recorded turns. Every shipped profile now pins 16,384, where the budget is about 32,522 minus the system prompt. TURN_RESULT_CHARS = 20,000 therefore no longer sits just under the budget; it now binds well below it, which is the opposite of the fault it was written for (rota/core/runner.py:410-430, rota/llm/profiles/local.toml:16).

The PUSH_CHARS comment says the pushes budget themselves at code.area 14,000, and code.area's actual budget is 10,000 with a comment arguing explicitly against 14,000 (rota/core/runner.py:406 against rota/roles/api.py:6024, 6018-6022). The backstop was sized against a number that the op itself had already rejected.

The one number a test asserts already has a written-in exception. The first code.source of a turn takes SOURCE_CHARS whatever the turn's room says, and the comment says _cap_exchange absorbs the overrun (rota/core/runner.py:2305). So a turn can exceed TURN_RESULT_CHARS by design, and the overrun is then cut by a different cap with a different wording.

Two notices in the same prompt contradict each other, and the code says so and leaves it open. The eviction notice says re-read anything you still need; the repeat line says the answer is above. Measured across 8,183 recorded prompts, all 8 that carry the eviction notice also carry the repeat line (rota/core/runner.py:2366-2376).

Five wordings exist for what is one event. The wake cut says the rest did not fit the window, the eviction says exchanges were dropped, the exchange cut says characters of this exchange did not fit, _render says TRUNCATED after N of M characters, and the withholding says this turn has no room left. A pushed read cut at PUSH_CHARS is told to ask for the next range, which a push has no range for (rota/core/runner.py:478, 486, 500, 707, 2308).

Only one of the caps pays for its own notice out of its limit. _exchange_cut does, and its docstring says that is so _fit can promise a number a test can assert; _render does not, which is why a separate 300-character reserve exists at the top of every turn (rota/core/runner.py:498-517, 436, 2156).

The record side truncates silently at four different lengths for one verdict. A break writes the quote at 300, the reason at 460, and copies both into the ledger at 160 each, so the principal's ledger can carry a shorter account than the challenge row it derives from (rota/roles/api.py:7091-7097).

The overflow detector is pure reporting. truncated is computed and written into the run's errors, and nothing retries, widens or re-sends (rota/llm/llm.py:416, rota/core/runner.py:1990-2001). The prompt side is the only side that adapts.

report.question: Trace how a prompt is assembled for one wake: the building function, every part, the order, the last function that sees all parts, whether one place holds the whole prompt before the send, and where num_ctx comes from at that moment.
report.summary: `build_prompt` at rota/core/runner.py:242 builds the prompt as two separate strings, a system string and a user string. The system string is one expression at runner.py:255-312 and holds six parts in this order: the composed brief, the identity paragraph, the tool signature list, the TOOL: protocol, the id rule, and the turn rule. The user string is a list joined at runner.py:367 and holds, in order: the wake kind, the inbound message line, the refs, the subject word, the wake detail, the inbound JSON, and the pushed read results. Yes, one place holds the whole prompt before the send: the `payload["messages"]` list at rota/llm/llm.py:355-358, inside `OllamaBackend.complete`. That place is transport only. It measures nothing, holds no budget, and the tool schemas join the same payload at llm.py:359-360 outside every budget. No place measures the whole prompt before the send: `run_session` computes one character budget at runner.py:1965 from `num_ctx` and `len(system)`, then fits only the transcript at runner.py:1972, and the only whole-prompt measurement is the estimate at llm.py:415, after the reply comes back. `num_ctx` at that moment is `pins.num_ctx`, set by `routed_pins` at runner.py:1766 from the run profile's per-role `context` map, and `run_session` still holds the `Wake` object in scope there, while `_fit_budget`, `_fit` and `backend.complete` receive only ints, strings and `Pins`.

open_questions: What would have to change for one place to hold and size the whole prompt before the send: a single object that carries the system string, the user string and the tool schemas together, built before `backend.complete` and measured there. The smallest change the code permits is to move `_fit_budget` and `_fit` behind a new function that takes that object and `pins.num_ctx` and returns a fitted object. That function would be the one place. `build_prompt` would return the object instead of a tuple at runner.py:367, `run_session` would pass it at runner.py:1975, and each backend would flatten it into its own payload. This is an inference from the call graph, not an observed plan.
The tool schemas at llm.py:359 reach the server and consume window. No code in this repository counts them. Whether they are large enough to matter is unmeasured here.

`_fit` promises the budget in its fast path (runner.py:596) but `_cap_exchange` floors (runner.py:538, 543) and the first source read (runner.py:2303) can each push the transcript past it. Which of the three actually fires on a night is unmeasured in the code I read.

The number a test could assert today is `len(system) + len(user) <= _fit_budget(num_ctx, len(system)) + len(system)`, that is `int(num_ctx / 2 * 3.97)`. Whether that is the number the design should pick, or whether the design should assert against the whole window instead of half of it, is a ruling I did not find in the code.
`routed_pins` keys the per-role window by `wake.role` (runner.py:126). Whether a window should vary by mode or by wake kind as well is not decided anywhere I read.
Where the LiteLLM and cassette paths would get the same whole-prompt check is unclear. Only `OllamaBackend.complete` computes `estimate` and `truncated`.
surprises: The system prompt is never cut. It is only subtracted from the budget at runner.py:566. An oversized brief plus an oversized signature list drives the budget to its 2000-character floor, and the transcript pays the whole price while the brief pays none.

There IS a single object holding the whole prompt before the send, at llm.py:355-358, but it is inside the transport, below every budget. The frame implies no such place exists. The real gap is not assembly. It is that nothing measures the assembled object before it goes.
The only whole-prompt measurement in the send path runs AFTER the reply (llm.py:415). The system learns the prompt did not fit from the answer it already paid for.

The output cap and the window are unrelated numbers. num_predict is 8192 (llm.py:319) against a default num_ctx of 12288 (llm.py:43), and Ollama's num_ctx covers prompt plus generation. The prompt budget already takes half the window, so the two caps together exceed the window by design.

Three different characters-to-token ratios live in the repository: 3.97 in `_fit_budget` (runner.py:566), 3.97 in the Ollama estimate (llm.py:415), and 4 in the cockpit preview (progress.py:480). The first two agree. The preview a person reads does not.

PUSH_CHARS is 20000 per pushed key (runner.py:366), with no total. A role with four pushed reads can put 80000 characters into the wake block before `_fit` ever runs. `_fit` then allows the wake up to two thirds of the budget (runner.py:596), which at a 12288 window is about 16000 characters.

`build_prompt` is called from two places (runner.py:1851 and progress.py:473). The cockpit path builds the same prompt for display and applies none of the runner's budgets, so what a person inspects is not what a session is sent.

report.question: What does _fit trim, in what order, what does it refuse to touch and why, what is its early return, what did frame 43's repair 4 change, and which of its behaviours would one priority-ordered budget replace or must survive?
report.summary: `_fit` trims in three stages: the wake first, then the middle of the transcript, then the latest exchange. It cuts the wake to two thirds of the budget, packs older blocks newest-first into what is left, and cuts the last two blocks last. It refuses to drop the first block and the last two blocks, because the brief lives at the front and an overflowing prompt is cut from the front by the server. Its early return is `sum(len(t) + 2 for t in transcript) <= budget`, and it then returns the same list unchanged. Frame 43's repair 4 changed three return statements only, so each one now calls the new `_cap_exchange`. Repair 4 added `_cap_exchange`, `_exchange_cut` and `_MIN_EXCHANGE`, and it left the middle eviction and its four-block guard untouched on purpose. One budget allocated down a priority order would replace the fixed two-thirds wake fraction, the half-each exchange share, and the second allocation that `run_session` computes at line 2154. Four behaviours must survive because they protect something an allocation does not: the cut notices, the cut direction, the floors under a part, and the slice guards.

open_questions: Inference, not fact: a budget allocated down a priority order would replace four things in `_fit`. The two-thirds wake fraction at :596, the half-each share at :542, the `_MIN_EXCHANGE` lend-back branches at :543-546, and the duplicate allocation at :2154. Each of these is a fixed fraction or a fixed literal where an allocator would compute a number from what the ranked parts ask for. Roman must rule whether that replacement is in frame 46's scope.

Inference, not fact: the packing loop at :618-622 is already an allocation. It spends the remaining room newest-first and stops at the first miss. A priority order would keep this rule as the middle's own rank and would not remove the loop.

Inference, not fact: four behaviours must survive a redesign because they protect something a budget does not. 1. The three cut notices (`_render_cut`, `_dropped_note`, `_exchange_cut`) tell the model what it lost and how to ask again. An allocation decides an amount and says nothing. 2. The cut direction: the wake keeps its head because the server cuts the front, so `_fit` must cut the back. Direction is not an amount. 3. The floors: `_MIN_EXCHANGE` 2000 and `MIN_RESULT_CHARS` 400 mark the size below which a part stops being useful, and below `MIN_RESULT_CHARS` the result is withheld whole rather than served as a stub. A proportional split has no such threshold, which is the F2 defect. 4. The slice guards at four and three blocks protect list arithmetic, not the budget, and a test pins them.

Open: does the one budget charge the tool schemas? They are sent at `rota/llm/llm.py:360` and are not in `_fit_budget`. This session did not measure their rendered size, and it did not confirm that ollama templates them into the prompt tokens.

Open: what is the one number a test can assert? Today two numbers compete. `_fit` promises `sum(len(b) + 2) <= budget`, which `tests/rota/test_runner.py:1251` asserts. The turn's results promise `TURN_RESULT_CHARS`, which is 20,000 and can exceed the budget of 20,391 by itself. A single budget must decide which of the two is the assertable number.

Open: can the priority order preserve byte-identity for a fitting transcript? The cassette key hashes the joined transcript at `rota/llm/cassettes.py:118`, and frame 43 measured that a re-key stales thousands of recordings. A design that rebuilds the list on every turn pays that price.

report.question: Find every place that tells a seat, a page, or a record that something was cut, trimmed, elided, truncated, held, or unchanged. Quote the exact string, say which names the tool that fetches the rest, and which leave no way to recover.
report.summary: I found 18 distinct strings that tell a seat something was cut, held, or unchanged, plus 3 silent cuts that tell it nothing. Only four strings name a call that fetches the rest: `_render`'s code.source extension, the landing page's `rows_not_shown` (names `rulings.line`), and the `not_shown` keys of `code.area` and `code.front` (both name `code.source`). Three cut functions in runner.py keep three different contracts: `_render_cut` and `_render` add the notice outside the limit, and `_exchange_cut` pays for it inside the limit. `_render_cut` has one string, "the rest of your wake ... did not fit the window", and two callers: `_fit` at line 598 cuts the wake, and `run_session` at line 2029 cuts the seat's own reply at a literal 4000 characters, where the word "wake" is wrong and no tool can fetch a reply back. The repeat line "OK {name} -> unchanged since you asked earlier this session; the answer is above." sits at runner.py:2403, and its sibling at 2400 is "OK {name} -> was run for you before you started; the answer is in the list above."; the pushed-key sibling is chosen when the key is in `pushed_keys`. The code carries a measured, deliberately open hole: the repeat line contradicts `_dropped_note` on 8 of 8,183 recorded prompts. Three cuts are fully silent: the fourth and later copies of one key in one turn get no line, the `substr(text,1,120)` headline columns say nothing, and `_as_table` flattens newlines to spaces. Every pushed result goes through `_render` at PUSH_CHARS, so a cut push says "Ask for the next range", and a push has no range.

The three cut functions in runner.py prove it: `_render_cut` and `_render` add the notice outside the limit, and `_exchange_cut` pays for it inside the limit, so three functions that do the same job keep three different contracts.

report.question: What does it cost to change a number in this system? Which numbers key a cassette, what turns stale when the window changes, what actually turned stale in frame 43, and what test seam and cheapest assertion exist around prompt assembly?
report.summary: A cassette key holds six values: model, temperature, num_ctx, protocol, the system text and the user text. The register's stale report reads none of them. `casestatus` matches on case id, prompt hash and model only, and the prompt hash digests the composed brief alone. So `num_ctx`, the temperature, and the tool signatures inside the system text all re-key every recording while the stale line stays silent. Frame 43 avoided that cost: it raised eight shipped profiles to 16384 and left `DEFAULT_NUM_CTX` at 12288, so nothing turned stale and all 18435 recordings kept their keys. The price is that the register replays at 12288 while a night runs at 16384. The prompt assembly seam is `build_prompt`, which returns `(system, user)` and takes no window at all. The cheapest number a test can assert is `(len(system) + len(user)) / 3.97` against the profile's window, and two such tests already exist, both against the literal 6100.

Night 87 used only one window, 16384. Every distribution here is conditional on that window and on the frame 43 caps. I cannot say from this data how the parts would grow if the budget rose.

The pushed working set dominates at the 90th percentile because vision_keeper and developer sessions push large source reads. Whether that holds for a different area or a different repository is untested.

verdicts.claim: The 3.97 ratio is 1.2 per cent low against the one prompt with a real server count (night 86 s168 turn 14, 48082 characters, server 12261 against estimate 12111).
verdicts.correction: s168 seq 14 is 5265 + 42817 = 48082 characters, 48082/3.97 = 12111, and 48082/12261 = 3.9215, a 1.22 per cent under-count. One placement correction: the note text lives in the completion of s168 seq 15, an empty-prompt row, not in turn 14's own row. The claim that this is the only usable server count is right for the wrong reason the report does not state: the other 14 notes in night 86 all report used = 6146, the collapsed half-window count, which carries no ratio.

verdicts.claim: tiktoken cl100k_base on 300 spread night-87 prompts gives a median of 4.243 characters per token, so the runner over-counts by 6.9 per cent.
verdicts.correction: Direction and size hold. On my sample (rowid order, every 12th of the 3599, n=300) the median is 4.261, the mean 4.180 and the range 3.417 to 4.613, giving a 7.3 per cent over-count. The reported range endpoints (3.486 to 4.708) do not reproduce, so the sample selection differs.

verdicts.claim: The part accounting closes: 3080 of 3599 turns sum within 8 characters, unattributed text is 0.18 per cent, median residual 4 and p90 10.
verdicts.correction: Not reproducible from the description: the report does not say which separators and notes are subtracted. My reconstruction gives a median residual of 8 characters, a p90 of 20, only 1863 of 3599 turns within 8, and 3.0 per cent of all prompt characters unattributed. The residual claim is the one that underwrites facts 13, 14 and 15, and it is the weakest-evidenced item in the report.

verdicts.claim: A 30-turn spread sample agrees with the full population: prompt median 4613, p90 7466, largest 8007; pushed 1132/5428/5472, the same three numbers as the full population.
verdicts.correction: The sample is every 119th row in rowid order, which yields 31 turns, not 30. Its p90 (7466) and maximum (8007) reproduce exactly, and the pushed working set reproduces exactly at 1132 / 5428 / 5472, matching the full population. The prompt median is 4583 tokens (median 18196 characters), not 4613.

verdicts.claim: Night 86 ran at 12288 and its largest prompt was 27155 tokens, so frame 43 cut the ceiling by a factor of 3.3.
verdicts.correction: Night 86: all 203 sessions at num_ctx 12288, 825 non-empty prompts of 937 turn rows, median 3515 tokens (report says 3516), p90 6104 (report says 6105), maximum 27155. probes/frame43/README.md line 76 carries "The largest is s71 at 27155 tokens". 27155/8191 = 3.32.

missed: The filter that takes the turns table from 4062 rows to 3599. 463 rows hold an empty system and user with a "SESSION ENDED. The runner's account:" completion. Excluding them is correct, but the report never names the filter, so no reader can reproduce 3599, 746 or any percentile from it.

rota/core/runner.py `_cap_exchange` (496-551) and `_fit`'s `len(transcript) < 4` branch (606-607). The whole "capped at half the window" finding rests on these, and the report cites only `_fit`'s early return at 586, which proves nothing about the cap.

The `max(2000, ...)` floor inside `_fit_budget` (line 566). The half-window ceiling breaks once the system prompt passes int(num_ctx/2*3.97) - 2000 characters, 30522 at 16384. Night 87's largest system is 10141 characters, so it never bound, but the report states the cap unconditionally and never says what would break it.

rota/core/runner.py:2154-2157, `result_room = min(TURN_RESULT_CHARS, max(budget - len(user) - len(completion.text) - 6 - _CUT_NOTE_CHARS, _MIN_EXCHANGE))`. This is where the six caps actually meet the budget, and it is the direct refutation of fact 17's "none was derived from the others". The report lists the constants and never reads where they bind.

rota/llm/llm.py:406, `used = body.get("prompt_eval_count") or 0`. A real server token count already exists in the runner. It contradicts "3.97 is the only token count the runner has" and it is the same field fact 20 uses.

Where the truncation note is stored. `outcome.errors` at runner.py:1997 lands in a turn row with an empty prompt (night 86, s168 seq 15). Fact 6 looks for it in the sessions table, which could never hold it. The verifying query is `turns.completion like '%prompt did not fit%'`, which returns 0 for night 87 and 15 for night 86.

The 67 turns whose stored user does not start with the session's first wake, and the 211 turns carrying `_render_cut`'s "the rest of your wake" note. The push distribution is measured from the seq-1 wake, so a cut wake would be counted at full size. I corrected for it and no push figure moved, but the report never tested the assumption its biggest finding rests on.

A stated, reproducible rule for splitting reply blocks from results blocks in the stored user string. Facts 12, 13, 14, 15 and 22 all depend on it, and none of their tail numbers reproduces. This is the report's one unverifiable method, and it carries the composition finding.

Evidence that night 87 ran the text protocol. `backend.complete(system, user, pins, tools=schemas)` at runner.py:1975 passes schemas, and the report asserts the text protocol in an open question with no citation from the night's own config or sessions rows.

The sessions.model column. The 3.97 ratio is justified in the code as "the measured ratio for these models", and the report never says which model night 87 ran, so the divisor is never tied to the night it is applied to.
